leading_positions.synthesis: Five members prefer a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye, with citations that all name the invention and its realization at the 1e-18 level. Eriksson (from B043), Mehlig (from B001) and Olsson (from B015) moved to B013 after reading the other ballots, while Kroll and Lindroth opened with it first. They share the view that attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and that independent confirmation makes maturity secure. They differ in how they treat overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, in whether the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice narrowly or precision optical clocks broadly, and in how far the pending redefinition of the second matters. Olsson explicitly says she prefers B013 for defensible attribution rather than because it outweighs the Higgs observation in significance. Kroll flags a possible perceived tie to the group around Jun Ye.

Three members prefer a single-part prize for the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson with ATLAS and CMS. They agree on the science: two independent detectors, a result stable through Run 1 to Run 3, and no experimental recognition after the 2013 theory prize. They name three different trios from the four credited leaders. Danielsson proposes Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee; Johansson proposes Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni; Pearce proposes Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee. Gianotti and Jenni appear in all three, and Danielsson and Pearce differ from Johansson only in Virdee versus Della Negra. Each of the three says the choice is a judgement on leadership not a verified accounting, and each lists B013 as an alternative (Danielsson and Johansson explicitly as a fallback). Mehlig, Lindroth and Olsson also hold the Higgs as a first alternative or as the larger result in significance, but have not made it their preferred configuration.

areas_of_agreement: Every member's preferred configuration is a single-part prize. Five choose B013 and three choose B001. No other ballot is anyone's preferred configuration in round 1.

B013 is the only shortlisted entry ranked by all eight members at opening. Members of both camps describe the same two-person allocation: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and early strontium clocks, Ye for the record-precision realization.

All eight members list B013 or B001 among their alternatives or preferences, and B001 and B013 are each other's alternative in most ballots (Danielsson, Johansson, Pearce, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson cite the other). Members who prefer B013 do not dispute the scientific significance of the Higgs discovery.

Members on both sides say that the Higgs observation has had no experimental recognition since the 2013 theory prize, and that its scientific maturity is not in question; the open issue is attribution.
Several members say the committee should settle credit by an explicit principle (for example founders versus spokespersons at the time of discovery) and not by counting proposals or votes.
scientific_disputes: Whether the scale and consequence of the Higgs observation should outrank the cleaner but narrower optical lattice clock invention, as Danielsson, Johansson and Pearce argue, or whether defensible attribution should weigh more, as Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson argue.

Whether optical lattice clocks are a distinct invention (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, many-body clock physics) or a refinement of the lineage already recognised in 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (ion control). Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Eriksson argue distinctness; Pearce, Danielsson and Olsson say the overlap cuts against novelty.
How secure the IceCube result (B059) is as a prize candidate. Pearce lists it as an alternative; Danielsson, Johansson and Lindroth rank it lower because source identification is still developing.

Whether B046 (twisted bilayer graphene), B044 (topological insulators) and B043 (DMFT) are mature enough. Lindroth, Eriksson and Olsson regard B046 as promising but early; Danielsson and Olsson see an overlap of B044 with the 2016 prize.
attribution_disputes: B001: with four credited names and a three-person limit, the three supporters propose two different trios, and the other five members see no defensible way to leave one founder out. Gianotti and Jenni are shared by all three supporters; the contested seat is Virdee (CMS, spokesperson at the time of discovery) versus Della Negra (CMS founding leader). Johansson's trio gives ATLAS two names and CMS one, and Pearce's and Danielsson's give the reverse. Members have also cited an earlier opening trio of mine (Gianotti, Della Negra, Virdee) that differs from my current round-1 proposal.

B013: whether the two names Katori and Ye fully reflect the people responsible, given contributions from Lemonde and the Paris group, the German groups (Lisdat, Sterr), Takamoto, NIST and JILA team members and the ion-clock pioneers. Lindroth and Olsson say the citation should be worded around the invention and its realization.
B046: Lindroth credits only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, while Johansson and Olsson say that dropping Bistritzer is hard to justify.
B044: Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson note that omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang leaves a significant gap, because the HgTe experiment followed their proposal.
B043: Eriksson and Johansson note that Metzner is not among the credited names.
maturity_disputes: B013: whether the redefinition of the second, still pending, strengthens the case if it takes place before the decision, or whether the practical payoff is still too prospective (Danielsson, Eriksson, Kroll, Mehlig, Olsson).
B001: whether the evolving Higgs-sector programme argues for waiting; Pearce, Danielsson and Johansson judge the discovery itself secure and will not be revised.
B046: whether the superconducting mechanism is still debated and the field only about eight years old (Eriksson, Lindroth, Olsson), against the clean theory-and-experiment pairing.
B059: whether the diffuse flux is secure but the source picture (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is still developing (Danielsson, Johansson, Lindroth, Pearce).

B054: Johansson and Mehlig note the proximity of circuit QED to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and Mehlig adds that the Girvin omission weakens attribution relative to B013.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Kroll: possible perceived tie to John Hall's laboratory, with which Jun Ye is associated (B013), described as not a documented conflict; Kroll says the committee may wish to consider recusal on B013. Eriksson and Mehlig note that support for B013 does not depend on Kroll's ballot.
Johansson: director of WACQT at Chalmers with research in circuit QED; he would recuse himself from deciding B054. Olsson asks that he not carry the scientific case for B054.

Olsson: electron microscopist and past president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, with close subject-matter proximity to B015; she would recuse herself from decisions on it and no longer pushes it.

Lindroth: documented collaboration with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, where Wallraff (B054) is based, and field proximity to cold-atom lattices (B050); she would recuse herself from these ballots if the committee judged it a conflict. She reports no conflict for B013.
Eriksson: subject-matter closeness to B043 and to the electronic-structure side of B044 and B046, with no personal link to credited candidates; he discounts his earlier support for B043.
Pearce (chair): no documented tie to ATLAS, CMS or any credited B001 name; field proximity, not a documented tie, to astroparticle entries such as B059 (IceCube), which is an alternative of mine.
questions_for_round2: B001: if the committee considers the Higgs discovery, what principle selects three of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee (founding conception versus spokesperson at the time of discovery), and can the supporters agree on one trio?
B001: is a leadership-based prize for a collaboration-scale discovery acceptable to members who now prefer B013 (Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson), and what evidence would change their mind?

B013 versus B001: do the B013 supporters rank the cleaner attribution above the larger significance of the Higgs discovery, and do the B001 supporters accept B013 as a fallback if no trio can be agreed?

B013: how should the citation separate the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 realization from the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes, and should it name neutral-atom lattice clocks narrowly or precision optical clocks broadly?
B013: does the pending redefinition of the second change the maturity argument in either direction, and should the committee wait for it?
B013: should the committee record Kroll's disclosed tie to Hall's laboratory as a recusal question, and would Kroll's recusal change any member's view of B013?

Is a two-part prize combining B001 and B013 worth considering, given Pearce's open question and the three-laureate cap, or should it be excluded because it would force a narrower laureate set for the Higgs part?
Should B046 (with Bistritzer credited), B044 or B059 be kept alive as alternatives, or is the committee deciding between B013 and B001 only?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 narrows the field to two single-part options with no overlap in laureates: B013 (Katori and Ye) with five explicit supporters and a stable two-name allocation, and B001 (the Higgs discovery) with three supporters who agree on the science but name different trios. Three of the five B013 supporters moved to it from another opening first place after reading the ballots, and all supporters of B001 name B013 as an alternative. The central question for round 2 is whether a defensible Higgs attribution can be stated as a principle, since the disagreement is about names and framing and not about the merit of either discovery. In the interest of accuracy, the member statements cite an earlier opening trio of mine that differs from my round-1 proposal; I have not altered any member statements.
